newsitem.title: USA: Cohen says no reason to change military training.
newsitem.headline: Cohen says no reason to change military training.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said Thursday he was content to allow military men and women to train together but that he was open to suggestions about it.

Cohen, making his first trip since taking over his new job Jan. 24, also told reporters after touring Lackland Air Force Base that the Pentagon had not handled very well the issue of illness among Gulf war veterans.
He made his comments after watching male and female recruits training together at Lackland, which is the Air Force's top training facility.

"Based upon my observations here today, it seems very clear to me that the Air Force has a very good training programme and it works well for the Air Force ... one would have to come up with some very compelling evidence why it should be handled differently," said Cohen, a former U.S. senator from Maine who is the only Republican in President Clinton's cabinet.

Joint training by military men and women came under fire Wednesday from Representative Bob Livingston, a Republican from Louisiana, who said it had led to sexual harassment, rape, pregnancy, divorce and sensitivity sessions that detracted from war readiness.

The U.S. military has been rocked in recent months by sexual harassment scandals at various bases, including Lackland. In November 1996 Air Force General Robert Courter said eight male instructors had been disciplined at the base since 1994 for improper relations with female recruits.
But Cohen has said that any changes in joint training must not cause women to lose gains they have made in the military.
"Right now, it appears we have the right mix...I have an open mind, but I have seen no compelling evidence that warrants changing (it)," he said.

Also, in response to reporters' questions, Cohen said the Gulf War illness controversy had been mishandled from the start. Gulf War troops have complained of symptoms ranging from memory loss to muscle aches, but the cause of the ailments remained unclear.

"The entire Gulf War illness programme was not originally handled well," he said. "There were records that were destroyed, information that was not shared, and I think the whole response on the part of the Pentagon was inadequate," he said.
